definition: Salinization means the gradual buildup of salt in soil or water.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word salinization. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know salinization should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even houseplants suffer salinization in miniature: years of tap water leave a pale rim of minerals that scorches the roots.
A trace of salt is far milder than salinization — detectable and harmless, the background level every field and well carries.
Sterility goes further than salinization — salinization is the buildup that cuts what land can grow; sterility is land past growing anything at all.

Salt buildup is the plain-words name for what salinization names formally: salt slowly accumulating where it does not belong. A farmer says the field has salt buildup; the extension office's report says salinization. The process is identical — only the audience changes.

Salary descends from Latin salarium, a Roman soldier's salt allowance — salt and pay were once close enough to share a word.
Salinization means the gradual buildup of salt in soil or water.

Two neighboring plots, one canal, and a lesson in salinization the extension office photographs every August: the grower who paid for gravel drains still cuts hay off his land, while the plot across the fence — same water, same sun, ten years of skipped drainage — has gone to gray-green scrub that only sheep will touch.
Salt did not arrive; it was delivered, a little with every watering, and it never left.

Salinization is the exact word for that slow delivery, because salinization means the gradual buildup of salt in soil or water — no spill, no single villain, just arithmetic: the canal water carries in a little dissolved salt, the sun takes the water and leaves the salt behind, and the ledger only runs one direction.
Erosion carries soil away; salinization ruins soil right where it stands.
Salinization lives in soil reports and river-basin studies; nobody reaches for it at dinner.
Its everyday neighbors are plain phrases — salt buildup, going salty.

The oldest farming records we can read are also a warning.
Clay tablets from ancient Sumer track four centuries of harvests on the same irrigated plain, and scholars can watch the trouble arrive in the arithmetic.
Each flood season, the canal water left behind a little of the mineral it carried; with no winter rains to flush the fields, salinization advanced a few finger-widths of soil at a time.
Wheat, the more sensitive crop, slips from the records first, replaced by hardier barley; then even the barley yields thin, generation after generation.
By the tablets' end, scribes describe once-productive fields glittering white and given over to weeds.
The plain did not fail in a season; it failed by degrees, too slowly for any one farmer to see.
